utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, after a long period, to everyone in this courtroom and good morning to everyone, those -- everyone outside the courtroom as well. We had a bit of a bad start, but let's resume properly. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The late start this morning was caused by technical problems which prevented us to start this hearing. I hope that they have been overcome now for sure. Are there any preliminary matters to be raised? I was not informed about any. Then is the Defence ready to call its next witness, and we understand that it would be Mr. Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher escort Mr. Gojkovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that -- apparently there's some audio ... Do you hear me now in a language you understand? Is it a channel or is it a -- do you now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation][No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The volume now having been adjusted. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojkovic. Please be seated. Mr. Gojkovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. In a minute he will be standing. He is. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your first and last name for the transcript. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Gojkovic, Dragic, son of Miroslav --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters could not hear the rest of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I invite you to speak a bit more slowly because already part of your last answer was not caught by the interpreters. Could you please repeat what you said after you said: "I'm Dragic Gojkovic, son of Miroslav ..." And what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Kosovo, in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Gojkovic, I was also informed that you might wish to consult some papers you've brought with you. If that is the case, please inform me that you want to consult any papers you brought; and, second, tell us what it is that you're consulting. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Lukic will now proceed. And if you keep the speed under control, there may be no need for further interpretations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was probably my mistake. I should inform Your Honours that consultation with the Prosecution, Mr. Gojkovic has his expertise in front of him and expertise of Mr. Riedlmayer, and it was checked by Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all fine, but we should know it and we now do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens, 1D5893, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, we have your CV in front of us. Has anything changed in the meantime since the time that you wrote this version of your CV, this draft of your CV?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is it correctly recorded here? Everything that has to do with your work history, is it correctly recorded according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this CV of Mr. Gojkovic into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5893 receives number D1170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1170 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens 1D5892, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, we see your report here that you drafted for this case. You're a member of the VRS. We were able to see that from your CV. I wanted to ask you when did you first begin to work on the damaged and destroyed buildings that are the subject of yours and Mr. Riedlmayer's analysis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: From the point of time when I was given the task of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you that when I'm pausing, it doesn't mean that I'm not satisfied with your answer. It just means that I'm waiting for the interpretation. During the war, were you given the task of working in any way on these destroyed religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not a part of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you look at the work of Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak clearly. The interpreters didn't catch your answer. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I looked at everything, absolutely. And I worked on that subject. I'm talking about the report of the expert Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is, of course, pretty obvious if you read the report that the witness did look at Mr. Riedlmayer's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had to have some introduction to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Lukic, that one of the previous questions were not answered. You asked when were you given the task, and -- I really don't know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't remember I asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think you asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said: "I wanted to ask you when did you first begin to work on the damaged and destroyed buildings...?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the answer was: "From the point of time when I was given the task of doing that." When was that? This is the critical question, I think. You should put that to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sometime in June 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, your reports starts with: "On 15 May 2014, I received the task from the defence team of the accused General Ratko Mladic..." And -- could it have been May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible. It's possible. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since I read that line anyhow, it also says that you not only received a task from the Defence team but also "a request of some wartime engineer officers of the VRS Army to review the part of the material..." that -- and then, et cetera. Could you tell us who they were? Who were the war-time engineer officers that requested you to do a similar thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was given the assignment from General Mladic's Defence team, I knew a number of the superior officers who were with me in the war, and there was talk about who could do it. Then they insisted that I do it because I'm the most senior among all the engineering superior officers in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I engaged some of those senior officers to help me in the drafting of the report because the deadline was very short to draft the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, you received the task. You then discussed with the others - four of them are mentioned in your report - who would take the lead, and then you decided that you would be the expert reporting and that the other four would assist you. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Looking at Mr. Riedlmayer's report, did you find out any data whether Mr. Riedlmayer established the material from which these destroyed buildings were built?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Except in a couple of places involving buildings made of stone where it was obvious by looking at the photographs that these were stone buildings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, could you repeat the last part of your answer and try to pronounce every word until the very end of your sentences. What was caught is that: "... it was obvious by looking at the photographs that these were stone buildings ..." And what did you then add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that the expert Riedlmayer noted in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that it was important to establish the construction material in order to be able to determine the manner of destruction, i.e., to determine the technology used in the destruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as an example, could you please tell us what is the difference between destroying reinforced concrete and a stone building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Each building constructed of any kind of material is different because the hardness of the material is different, the hardness of stone, of stone, of brick, of reinforced concrete requires a different approach in order to destroy such a building. This is how it's regulated. It's how you need to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to destroy a building, on the basis of the rules that you acted upon, you and the engineering units of the VRS, was it necessary to get the appropriate documents pertaining to such a project?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That is the very basis. You cannot move any further if you don't have the proper project documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apologies to interfere. But when reading your report, I found out there were all kind of rules and what is the proper way, well prepared to destroy a construction. I also noted that you established that in almost all if not all of the cases that was not what was done. It was done in the -- the fast way, to say, just put a lot of explosives in it and then blow it up. So, therefore, that may make it, Mr. Lukic, less relevant to look in detail to how it should have been done if it was done in accordance with the rules, because that's apparently what, if I understand your report well, was what never happened. Is that a proper understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So tell us what you should know if you would prepare it properly if it was never done seems to be of less, if any, relevance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Mr. Riedlmayer's papers, did you find anything to that effect, that he dealt with the project documentation, the plans of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for conclusions, except in relation to these two buildings that you have mentioned by way of an example, the Ferhadija mosque and the Petricevac monastery, on the basis of what did you draw conclusions in terms of how buildings were being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of reports by Mr. Riedlmayer, because I did not have any other access to these buildings. Even more so, because in the meantime all of these buildings were repaired, reconstructed, rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the dimensions? Now we're talking about mosques. What are the dimensions of most mosques in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 94 buildings that Mr. Riedlmayer dealt with in his report, except for the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka and the Aladza mosque in Foca, and its dimensions are 18.-something metres by 14.-something metres, most other mosques are 10 by 8 maximum and they are 5 to 7 metres high. So they're rather fragile edifices, especially when there is no reinforced concrete, when not built in a modern way, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask: Were they of them not built in a modern way; in other words, not built with reinforced concrete? You said you didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are quite a few. There were quite a few. You can see that from the photographs that are attached to Mr. Riedlmayer's report. When one looks at the photographs in detail, that can be seen, although it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say you can see by looking at the photograph that the building was not reinforced? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be seen, of course. I mean, you cannot be absolutely certain. But 90 per cent, yes. Ultimately, you can see that from some other information and that is the time of building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you managed to see this from photographs? Do explain this to us. On the basis of what did you manage to see that they were not built in a modern way, not reinforced, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are places of worship that are made of stone, and that can be seen. There are places of worship that are made of bricks, and that could be seen when they are destroyed. And then especially when minarets were destroyed, when the minaret was cut, if you will, then you see the reinforcement, and that can be seen just by looking at the photograph at first glance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 119 from this document that's on our screen. It's 1D5892. It's enough it's in B/C/S version. That's the picture I wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Gojkovic, what would you say on the basis of this photograph? Was this a reinforced building or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the mosque in Kamengrad, Sanski Most. The mosque was built just before the war, mostly made of reinforced concrete, as can be seen from the photograph itself. It was destroyed in a rather unprofessional way. The entrance of the mosque remained basically intact. Too much explosive was used here, but the explosive was not placed properly, and the preparation was not carried out in accordance with rules and standards that were applied by the former JNA because you see that the entire front side remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why is it important to know the size of a building and the construction of the building in terms of destruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely important because I claim with full responsibility that most destroyed facilities can be removed mechanically without explosives, without destroying buildings around them. So mechanisation can be used. There was no need for this kind of wild destruction as shown by the expert in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "mechanically," could you explain what you mean by that and what that presupposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it presupposes the use of appropriate machinery for a construction. Different types of construction depends on the element involved, which element one wishes to destroy on a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there is a difference in pages between the B/C/S version and the -- because you referred to page 119 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, yes. That's not -- and what page would that be in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second. Page 124 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 124, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have -- I'll ask first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your paper, the review of engineering units of the VRS, how did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As chief of engineering of the 1st Krajina Corps - and I assumed this duty in 1992, in October, sometime in October, and until 1997, I held that post. I, as chief of engineers, I left the complete archives I had to my successor, including all the work notebooks that I was issued in the beginning of every year, and I recorded all the tasks I received from my superiors; primarily from General Talic and General Kelecevic. I kept all of this in the archives. Now when I was given this task, I tried to find that, but I couldn't find anything. There's nothing left. These archives are not left. And I precisely recorded everything there, each and every word, and I left that in the archives of the corps and I couldn't find that. As for tables, it is correct. As for the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, I must admit that I know that very well, even 20 years later. I must admit that I don't remember some things. But as for the other units, we called some people and I managed to gather some information that way because I had no other way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 4 in English and page 5 in B/C/S of the same document, please. 4 in English and 5 in B/C/S. 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the B/C/S version here from the very beginning. And in the second half of the English page, there is a list of engineer units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move to another page in English, please. Next page. That's only continuation of the first, point 1. And then we need another page, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, when speaking of the Drina Corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, did you have immediate knowledge about these units or did you collect this information for the purposes of this paper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we contacted people from the 2nd Corps, the then-chief of engineering of the 2nd Krajina Corps, Colonel Milos Babic. As for the Eastern Bosnia Corps, we contacted Colonel Sokic. For the Drina Corps, I would kindly ask that the name not be mentioned because this is still an active-duty officer. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, for the time being, if the Trial Chamber feels that you need to mention the actual name, then we will move into private session, but now let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: For the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it was Colonel Avramovic who provided this information to me. And for the Herzegovina Corps, I received information again from the same person that was from the Drina Corps and that is now still an active-duty officer in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 7 in the B/C/S, because that's the first one on the left-hand side, and page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Lukic. I would like to hear from you, Mr. Gojkovic, what information did you receive from these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information about the engineering units that were in the units of the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, we see before us an analysis of VOB-8, the 1st Engineer Regiment of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS during the war. Sorry. Just a moment, please. I need to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have those documents introduced into e-court separately and as part of this work of Mr. Gojkovic, so I would kindly ask you to tell me which way would you prefer: To use documents already attached as part of the expertise, or do you want me to call up 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also looking at Mr. Traldi, whether he has any suggestions or preferences?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My recollection of the Chamber's decision on the 94 bis motion for Mr. Gojkovic was that the attachments to the report should be considered separately, and I think for the clarity of the record we need the 65 ter on the record when Mr. Lukic tenders if it he's going to do so. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be good, Mr. Lukic, because if there would be any dispute about any attached documents, any of the annexes to the report, then if we take them as a whole it's more difficult to decide on them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- refer to them as separate documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps in order to better understand the testimony, also state on the record that it is the same as an attachment to the report and which one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we have 1D5758, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that, Mr. Lukic, I think -- and I didn't hear from any of my colleagues, to insist on hearing the name of the person the witness referred to. But the mere fact that it's an active-duty officer, of course, if it is at the same time someone who is the source of knowledge of this expert witness, is in itself not sufficient to consider that as protected information. But again you didn't insist, the Chamber doesn't insist, but we still do not know whether Mr. Traldi would insist on hearing that name. Perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll consider it over the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, we see a document here entitled: "Analysis of VOB-8, 1st Engineer Regiment of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS During the War." Could you please tell us what this table shows, who drafted it, who filled in the information, and on the basis of what information was it created?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted the table. VOB-8s for the two engineering units I received from the Ministry of Labour of the government of Republika Srpska. I received the VOB-8s from the Ministry of Labour and the veterans' benefit service from the government of Republika Srpska. On of the basis of their data, I personally created the table. And the information in the table was entered by Lieutenant-Colonel Zeljko Strukar who was an operative in the 1st Engineers Regiment from mid-1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what can we see in the table?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The table indicates first how many soldiers from different ethnic groups passed through the units in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, and 1996. I mean Serbs, Croats, Muslims. Also, what the -- how many of them were transferred from the regiment units to different engineers units of the 1st Krajina Corps per year, year by year. The third column shows how many deserters were there from the regiment units, again by year and by ethnicity. I can't really see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged for the witness, or if you want to consult, I asked you to tell us, but you are now apparently consulting the paper copy. But it could be enlarged for you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's all right. All right. I'm. Then in the next column there are people who were demobilised because of work obligation, and the data is compiled by year and by ethnicity. And then the next column is the number of people who were killed by year from 1991 to 1995, by ethnic groups as well. And then there is the number of soldiers that survived until the end of the war, and the figure is given by ethnic group: So we have 92.7 Serbs or 1.649; there are 66 or 3.7 Croats; 63, or 3.6 percents Muslims. Total number is 1.778 soldiers. Now, why did I present this information? Primarily, you can clearly see in the table what sort of discipline there was in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what do you think? What was the discipline like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer in 1991 and 1992 and 1993, personally I was dissatisfied with discipline. We had a lot of problems in the working -- in working with the soldiers. And in 1994 and 1995, discipline was drastically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you again repeat the last part of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally believed that discipline in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1991, 1992, 1993 was not very high, and it was very difficult to work directly with the men in the field. Already in 1994 and 1995, the discipline was much better and much stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what sanctions were imposed on deserters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The punishment for desertion were that we reported it to the ministry or actually the military department. We reported what they did, what the measures were that were taken, what was done, so actually a very small number of these cases or these people were processed. And I just would like to emphasise here that literally Muslims and Croats who were leaving at the time were not subject to any kind of censure or punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 9 in the English version and page 8 in the B/C/S version of your report, a document is referred to as 1D -- JUDGE ORIE, Mr. Lukic, are you done with this document we had on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a question for the witness. Witness, could I take you to the column in which deserters are mentioned. And could it be enlarged slightly in the B/C/S so that I can also check whether there's any ... let me ... if you'd give me just one second to check whether there's any mistake here. Yes -- but could it be enlarged, just the deserter part; that is, which is now the -- right, but -- yes. And to be enlarged considerably. Yes. Could you have a look at that. I see that you are dealing with the totals and the percentages. Now, the total of deserters over all those years is: 80, which is 5.5 per cent, and then we're talking about Serbs; Croats, 15, which is 1 per cent apparently; and then Muslims, 51, 35 per cent. Now, I understood that the percentages in the vertical columns are such that they would cover the total number which then appears below. Could you explain to me how 5.5 per cent, plus 1 per cent, plus 35 per cent, makes up 100 per cent? Because for all the other vertical columns where totals are described, adding the percentages brings me to close to 100 per cent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct. Yes, Your Honour, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's mistake there, if I understand you well. And would it be that it should be for the 80 to be -- could -- if you'd. Could it be that for the 80 Serbs who deserted that that is approximately 55 per cent, that for the 15 Croats it's approximately 10 per cent, and that together with the 35 per cent of Muslims that you would come to 100 per cent, approximately? Is that how I have to reinterpret these percentages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, that's an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Numerically, no; but the percentage, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, to be so vigilant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would offer then this document to be MFI'd. Probably it would -- should -- those percentages should be corrected first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How we should do that is still -- or perhaps if the parties would agree on it, then later on we could perhaps make a new version of this document with the agreement of the parties implemented in it, and then of course it's not the document by the expert witness any further but it is a document agreed upon by the parties on -- initially based on the expert's table. Madam Registrar, the MFI number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5758 receives number D1171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, on the page of the expert -- Mr. Gojkovic's report, in English version 9, and in B/C/S version 8, we can find a document marked as 1D5759 and if we have this one on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, we see another table here, and it says the numerical overview of the movement of soldiers of the 1st Pontoon Battalion of the 1st Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. Could you please tell us who drafted the table, who filled in the information, and what does it -- what sort of information does it present.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The table is absolutely the same as the table of the 1st Engineers Regiment. I drafted it, and the information was entered into the table by Lieutenant-Colonel Zeljko Strukar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to have the English of the table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The English one is exactly the B/C/S version, the table itself, but the explanation in English should be -- if we turn the page, yes, then we have the English explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, it's a kind of an agenda for translating B/C/S into English, what the keys are. It's not very easy for us to work with, Mr. Lukic, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the first table was translated and the second one is not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither I do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will check who did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did not do it, exactly. But I still think it's easier, even for Your Honours, to see the table without keys than to see keys without the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It depends on the question what you want to do with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I already put my question, Your Honour, and I want to hear from our witness what's the importance of this document, how it was composed. He already said that he composed the chart, the table, and that somebody else filled it in. And if can he also explain what does it describes, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, could you please tell us, first of all, why did you separate the pontoon battalion from the 1st Engineers Regiment, why was there a separate table made, and could you please explain something about the table?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: These were two different -- two separate war units, independent ones, absolutely, which had separate war-time assignments. One is the engineers regiment's task and the other one is the pontoon battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us again something about the column of the deserters. We can see here that the calculation is correct in percentages. I think it's correct here. So could you please tell us again whether the fact that Muslims and Croats who had left the unit were not punished also applies to this unit or was the situation different in the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely, they were not punished. We did not even stop anyone from leaving the Army of Republika Srpska. If they wanted to leave, absolutely, whoever left -- whoever stayed, they could stay - I mean the Muslims and the Croats. But if they wanted to leave, we never stopped them. And I can also add something that's important here. Throughout the war, the 1st Krajina Corps Engineers Regiment chief of a section was Strukar, Zeljko, and then sometime until August another commanding officer was a Muslim. Things were absolutely clear in this matter. There was no discrimination at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would just offer this document before the break, and I can see that it's a break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we take that break, Mr. Lukic, the right side - that is, those remaining in the unit - has just disappeared on this -- it's just not there, which is -- it starts with "osta" and then under it "u je" and that is supposed to be at the far right side of this table and it disappeared. And it disappeared. You see that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do now.

utterances.text: So if you want us to consider these tables, then it should be complete tables, and the B/C/S version is not any better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see that now, yes.
