utterances.text: So, therefore, the Chamber would highly appreciate if before asking questions about tables you would look at them and to see what I see in one minute that they're incomplete. But then we'll take a break. Witness, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to use the time, Mr. President, I'd undertaken to consider over the break whether we did want to know the remaining name, and we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to know that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll invite the witness to -- Mr. Lukic, if I expressed what in itself would not be a sufficient reason to keep something confidential, is there any other matter which would support any such confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we should ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the witness gave the reason already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you earlier referred to a person you approached when you said you'd rather not give his name because he's still an active-duty officer. Now, that in itself is not a sufficient reason to not give his name. So if there are no other reasons to keep his name confidential, you're invited to tell us what his name is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. It is Colonel Sinnik [phoen] Zeljko, an engineer. He works in Sarajevo. That's it. He was company commander in the Zvornik Brigade otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you repeat the name. You said it was Colonel Zeljko. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sinnik is his last name, Zeljko is his first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to this MFI D1171, and we have proposed percentages: For Serbs, 80 should be 54.79; for Croat, 15 percentage should be 10.27; and for Muslims, 51 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One, second, Mr. Lukic. What exactly are we now dealing with? What column are we in? What --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Deserters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Deserters," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where we had wrong percentages, Your Honour. No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: But not the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have -- do not have the right document before us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have D1171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was marked for identification. And could it be ... deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under "deserters," column that starts on the left-hand side with 1: Serbs has number of 80, and the percentage should be 54.79 according to our calculations, and we expect the Prosecution to check it. Under column 2, Croats: Number is 15, percentage should be 10.27. In column 3, Muslims: Number of men is 51, and percentage should be 34.93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I said before, although not with that precision, that it would be 55, 10, and 35. That's -- but, of course, you now gave it in the further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are working on this, the next document we called, which is 1D5759. The last column was missing, where it should be shown how many men remained in the unit until the end of the war. So if we can MFI that one and hopefully we'll have the correct version by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D1172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly, the Prosecution has checked and accepts Mr. Lukic's calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, most of the percentages are not up to the lower -- the final digits, but lets leave it to that. It's now more or less accurate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it would be more clear, even those two lists, if we go through the next four documents, and I will call 65 ter number 1D5766. It's list of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity who were members of the 1st Engineering Regiment of the VRSK, 1st Krajina Corps, with the records of their movement during the war. In the report, those -- this document can be found in English version on page 52, and in B/C/S version on page 51 and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, do you see this? It is page 51, 53 of your report. It's a list that you can see on the screen here. It is soldiers of Muslim ethnicity who were members of the 1st Engineer Regiment of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska with records of their movement during the war. Could you please tell us who compiled this table on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I compiled the table on the basis of VOB-8; that is to say, a database that was kept in the 1st Engineer Regiment. This information was also entered for me by Lieutenant-Colonel Zeljko Strukar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Gojkovic, number 3, Arzemovic [phoen], Arzemovic, you say he was a member of the VRS from the 24th of September, 1991, to the 3rd of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the VRS in existence in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but then here you're not talking about the JNA. The heading says "Engineer Regiment of the VRS 1st Krajina Corps." So you're not talking about the JNA here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. But it was very hard to make a distinction through these lists. The engineer regiment was established on the 17th of September, 1991, and later on it became part of the 1st Krajina Corps. But it was a unit of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure most of the people who were in the VRS were former members of the JNA, but all I'm saying is that there was no such thing as the VRS in 1991. Anyway, we have noted the point. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you verify the accuracy of this data yourself, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about line 4, for instance. Let us deal with this document quickly on that basis. It says Alija Jasar, son of Redzo, 20th of May, 1992, that's when he came to the unit. The 22nd of June, 1992, that's when he left the unit. And it says "transfer."

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where it was that he was transferred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, regrettably I couldn't find that in the VOB-8 and that's why I didn't record it. It's probably a mistake on the part of the desk officer for the ORMOB, so I didn't want to forge anything. I simply copied what I found in the VOB-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 20 says Boric, Dzenad, and son of Fuad, from the 28th of May, 1992, only until the 1st of June, 1992. What does it say here? What is written there, the transfer to the 327th Inzb, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 327th Motorised Brigade in Derventa. The regiment received orders to establish an engineering battalion from parts of the regiment. Preparations for the corridor were underway then, and then we transferred part of our unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then and why does it say 327?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we first go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you please make a little pause between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So number 20, it says that 327th Inzb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 327th is a war-time unit of the former JNA that was renamed the 27th Motorised Brigade of the VRS in Derventa after mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 27th or the 327th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the question put by the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got the answer, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need to deal with it any further. So do you have anything to add with regard to this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On page -- actually, number 142. I actually highlighted that. This is an officer who until August 1992 was a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see page number 142, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, the number is 142. In terms of this list, that is the 142nd person on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S -- actually, we already have it. We already have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not in B/C/S yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the last number on this page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 142. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what you were talking about? Nalic, Ramo. It says that he deserted, that he left on the 10th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's a mistake. He was transferred to Belgrade. He had a problem. Some soldiers attacked him when they were on mission and after that we sent him to Belgrade, so the unit literally sent him to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he come back after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, he went to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the other information here, is that all right in this table?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this moment, we will offer this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5766 receives number D1173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, do you have any explanation compared to other data we've seen that the number of Muslim soldiers that are reported here as members of the VRS, either because they were already in the same units in the JNA or even sometimes entering after the beginning of the war, why the percentage was relatively high compared to what we've seen in other units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for other units in the Army of Republika Srpska, I really don't know what the situation was. I never dealt with that. I didn't look at this information. I didn't have an opportunity to do so. What is -- actually, those members of the Muslim and Croat peoples who went to war with us in September 1991, most of them stayed on with us until the end of the war. There's just one thing I need to tell you here: At the time, the chief of engineering in the 1st Corps was Colonel Hasanovic, who really insisted on that, to keep as many Muslims and Croats in the Army of Republika Srpska as possible. I personally and my colleagues after me, I think that we all treated these people very fairly and properly. To this day, I have very fair and good relations with these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question is: If I just look at the page which is on my screen now in the B/C/S, which goes from 90 to 142, I already see seven Muslim soldiers who joined the unit at the 9th of October, 1995. Could you tell us what specifically happened on that day that there was a -- well, relatively large influx of Muslim soldiers in the unit on the 9th of October, 1995, which was just before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were probably young people who were pursuing studies or their education and then they were mobilised and sent to these units. And also they were volunteers in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you earlier said: Well, we treated these people very well. Now the VRS was, if I could say so, in many instances involved in operations or military activity against Muslim units or Croat units. So, therefore, if you say we treated those Muslims well, that other factor, that the VRS was often involved in a military dispute with, apart from Croatian forces also Muslim force, remains. Do you have any explanation as to why Muslim soldiers apparently in larger numbers than as found elsewhere joined in an army which was engaged in many instances in military activity against Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, it was a very complex situation, and in a way it was different from area to area. We had a pretty clear situation in these units. We provided engineering support in combat, so our situation was pretty clear and we didn't have any problems to carry this out. As for combat assignments, we were carrying them out literally from the western Krajina area, the western part of the B and H, all the way down to Trebinje. I personally participated in all of that, and really I cannot speak about other units but that is my experience in these units, and I didn't have any problems like that. There was mutual confidence. These relationships were built right at the beginning, so we didn't have any problems with the people. Even people who were leaving the units, we saw them off fairly clearly. We parted on good terms. And there is one more thing. Testifying to the truthfulness of this is that the main operative in our staff throughout the whole war was a Croat, and nobody considered him to be any different than anybody else who was carrying out their combat assignments. This was the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question because I didn't understand one of your previous answers to the question of Judge Orie. You said with respect to the 9th of October, 1995: "These were probably young people who were pursuing studies or their education and then they were mobilised..." You said "they were probably young people." Do you have any factual knowledge or is it just an assumption? What is the significance of the 9th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this. I know from that time that a student brigade was formed, you know. A number of students were called up. They were mobilised. So I assume that a number of people from there came to my unit. That's all I can say. I don't have any other information. It is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have 1D5767 on our screens, please. And it's -- we can find that in the work of Mr. Gojkovic on the pages, in English version, 59, and page 55 in B/C/S version as Attachment I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see a list here of soldiers of Croatian ethnicity, and these are records of their movement during the war. These are members of the 1st Engineer Regiment of the VRS 1st Krajina Corps. We can see that the document ends with number 123. Under number 10, we see a bold entry. Is there any reason why some names are in bold?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Only to show the people who were in the unit until the end of the war. This means they stayed in the unit until the end of the war. Either they were people who were returned to the Ministry of Defence or who were discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "returned to MO," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It means that they were returned to the Ministry of Defence. Somewhere it's written "returned to the MO," and somewhere it says "discharged," so I didn't want to change the information which was already entered in the VOB-8, which you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are the officers on this list as well or was there a separate list for them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This list includes everybody: Officers, NCOs, and soldiers, all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And does this list contain only those soldiers of Croatian ethnicity or are there any others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's all soldiers of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence, Your Honour. We would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5767 receives number D1174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can see 1D5768 now, please. We can find that document on the pages, in English version, 64, and in B/C/S version, page 58. And it's Attachment K in the work of Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, we have a list here of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity who were members of the 1st Pontoon Battalion of the VRS 1st Krajina Corps with records of their movement during the war. Ferid Glisic is in the first row. He came to the unit on the 20th of May, 1992, left the unit on the 26th of February, 1996, and it says here that he was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The source of your information for this table, could you please tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was also the VOB-8 of the battalion. I just happened to know this person. He worked in a company in Gradiska, and the director called me and asked me to release him because he had to do something that had to do with a certain job. They couldn't do without him. So there were cases like that where the directors or presidents of municipalities would request that certain people be returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything characteristic about this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under entry number 19, is there the name Zoran Jazovic, son of Ibrahim. He came to me during the time of the JNA, I personally accepted him, and he stayed as commander of the amphibian company until the end of the war. He was literally carrying out assignments from the western part of the Krajina down to Bijeljina. He was a very good man, a technologist by profession, and I'm still on very good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence. I said we would offer this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5768 receives number D1175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have 1D5769 on our screens, please. And from the expert report of Mr. Gojkovic, it's on page 66 in English version and 59 in B/C/S version. It's Attachment L.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the 1st Pontoon Battalion. There is a list of soldiers of Croatian ethnicity with records of their movement during the war. Could you please tell us again what the source of the information is and who drafted the table, who entered the data?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted the table, and the sources are the records of the VOB-8 records, and Strukar Zeljko again was the one who entered the data into the table and I verified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything characteristic for this table?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here entry 30, Tomislav Sambol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page in both versions on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have Tomislav Sambol, entry 30. He was an NCO diver. And then again we have 33, Franc, Sasnja, he was Slovenian, also a diver. Right now is he a deputy in the council of the people in the Assembly of Republika Srpska -- the chamber of the people. They were in an action, and I would just like to mention it, they were saving a pontoon bridge from the territory of Croatia after an attack, and they were bringing the bridge to the other side, and this is something that they carried out successfully. There was another Croat who, along with some Serbs, took part in this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I just have a small -- a little bit of confusion. I'd understood this to be a list of ethnic Croatian as it was introduced. We had two examples given, and the only one of those that the witness gave an ethnicity for was Slovenian rather than Croatian. So I'm just curious if the witness could be asked if he verified the other ethnicities on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you briefly explore this matter, Mr. Lukic, and then we'll see the confusion still is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that my colleague has reminded me, I just wanted to ask you about Sasnja Franc. Where is he from? Is he from Croatia or from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He is a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear whether he was a Croat or a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked if he was a Slovenian by nationality or a Croat from Slovenia. I asked whether -- in B/C/S whether this gentleman --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Croat from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sasnja Franc is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Number 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a Slovenian by ethnicity or a Croat from Slovenia, and Mr. Gojkovic said that he -- he is a Croat from Slovenia and that he is, as a member of Croatian people, member of VRS assembly these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you referring to number 33 on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 33, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, chamber of the people, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, does this remove your concerns you expressed earlier? It was not a real opposition, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, it removes the confusion about that example. I'm just checking if the witness had said that he verified the other ones, which I don't think -- I'm not -- and he had, in fact, so I'll not object to admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5769 receives number D1176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, the previous two tables that we looked at, the summary tables, were they drafted on the basis of these four tables or on the basis of something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was done on the basis of the VOB-8. That was the database. I didn't look at anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I wanted to go back to your report, 1D5892.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 9 in the B/C/S and page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this part that is entitled: "Analysis of Training of Engineer Units of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska Between 1991 and 1995," the last paragraph in both versions reads as follows: "The engineer units of the corps were absolutely trained to carry out any combat tasks relating to engineering support for combat operations, including demolition of bridges, road sections, tunnels, embankments, buildings, and so on." You assert that on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The peacetime engineers regiment, the 293rd of the JNA, later on the first such regiment of the VRS, if there were to be an attack by the eastern bloc at the time, it would have held three key facilities on the Sava river and the task was to destroy them, if necessary; that was the bridge in Slavonski Brod; it was the bridge across the Sava river in Gradiska; and it was the bridge in Jasenovac that linked Slavonia, Bosnia, and Baranja. Regularly every two years a unit from there, a reserve unit, of course, would go to these facilities and simulate that demolition. That is one point. Another thing. In 1986, and I forgot to write that here, the commander of the peacetime regiment was a man who was later a general, Radivoje Tomovic, he is deceased. He carried out a methodological exercise in the village of Cerovljani at the request of the municipality of Gradiska to destroy a former JNA barracks, and he accepted that and he took advantage of that opportunity holding an exercise there to see how a housing facility is destroyed with all members of a war-time unit of the regiment. Of course, this is what officers were told, commissioned officers from lieutenant to colonel, and then we were all ordered to create the project documentation for that. And this man precisely, Zeljko Strukar, who was commanders of the pioneers company, was in charge of the actual demolition. It was filmed. A crew came from Banja Luka. I tried to find the footage; however, regrettably I didn't manage to. It's been misplaced somewhere and this exercise was a successful one, it was carried out, and there was this analysis. We were all pleased that it was all done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I [inaudible] on the record? Did you say in the municipality of? Where did this thing take place, in the municipality of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say another thing. The mentor of that exercise says was a colonel, Colonel Tomovic, who on several occasions was a member of peace missions with the JNA abroad. After the catastrophic earthquake in Banja Luka in 1979 [as interpreted] [Realtime error read "1997"], he personally demolished many buildings in Banja Luka. He is a man who had vast experience and we could learn a lot from him as we did. Truth to tell, he was retired at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The transcript says that the earthquake was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, it seems that you've have forgotten from before the summer recess that you should not speak aloud. It is now the second time today. Refrain from doing it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? When we worked with young recruits, training went on for six months, the final part of the training was with proper mines and explosives, and within that we destroyed elements, materials, and so on; that is to say, for example, rails, steel structures, et cetera. That was done with every group. But it is the reserve force that was focused on during this training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now heard a lot about the training and how to properly demolish a building or -- is there any dispute about VRS or JNA units being trained in properly doing it? Apart from how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Without speaking to which units or anything like that, Your Honour, there's certainly no dispute that some units in the VRS and JNA were trained pursuant to the JNA guide-lines on demolishing buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm intervening because, again, what seems to have happened, at least if we read the report of the expert well, which is not in accordance with the rule demolishing buildings, and so therefore to say whether they were trained, what the rules were, et cetera, apparently the only thing, and that seems to be not in dispute, is that the units who could have properly demolished the buildings were trained to do that. Whether they finally did the improper or the fast way of demolishing buildings, of course, is a totally different question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of your knowledge, if down the chain of command an order would arrive to destroy something, in Krajina which units would be in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, such an order, I mean, certainly would not have gone beyond the link in the chain where I was. Well, truth to tell, I received -- well, it was in July 1992 that I took over, and then in October 1992 I became chief of engineering. And then until July 1992, I was commander of the pontoon battalion, and at that time I held the point where the Sava was crossed to Western Slavonia. We were in Western Slavonia at that point in time. You see?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when were you there, in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Until -- until the beginning of July. So I got one unit out of Western Slavonia, and I sent them to -- to the corridor, Kotorsko, and a unit from Slavonski Brod left it. So I didn't even know where I was going. So this was before Operation Corridor. And part of the engineer units of the engineer regiment and the armoured brigade, they were still in Western Slavonia where they were taking care of minefields, de-mining them. We are thinking of that. We are getting rid of roadblocks and so on and so forth. I personally was taken aback by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you please look at your question at page 42, lines 17 to 19, and tell us whether you've got an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I haven't got an answer, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you likely to pursue that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gojkovic, if something was supposed to be demolished --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- legally --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- who would receive this order down the chain of command in the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of engineers. At that time, Colonel Kosanovic, who was chief of engineering at the time, who had to deal with this and send it to the subordinate units. So he was supposed to submit it to the commander for signature and then he would send it to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at page 11 in B/C/S and page 12 in English. That is number 7: "Organisation and Technology of Demolition in Urban Areas." Over here in the previous preparations for demolition, you mentioned all of that. You mentioned, like now, the order --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and you say gathering project documentation and so on and so forth. In the papers that you reviewed that were written up by Mr. Riedlmayer, did you notice something that had to do with one of the facilities that you dealt with during the these preparations? Was there an order? Was there project documentation that had been gathered. Did you find anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really did not find any such document. I reviewed everything, I read all of this, and really, it is a huge task, and you gave me this task for seven hours. And had I not taken a lot of people to work with me, I couldn't have handled this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what was allocated to you by the Registry and that is how the Defence has been functioning. As you were working on this report, did you look for project documentation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Truth to tell, when I was given this task, I was really tormented. I wondered where I should start from and what I should show here, which building I should deal with in greater detail and where I should calculate the minimum amount of explosives for the unhindered, if I can put it that way, leveling of the facility involved. I first addressed the town planning institute of Banja Luka because I wanted to work on the basis of Riedlmayer's report, and he mentioned Arnaudija, a mosque at Pobrdje that was destroyed twice; and at the same time within the scope of five minutes, it was totally destroyed together with the Ferhadija. I went to the institute there. And as -- they were looking for documentation for Arnaudija that Riedlmayer refers to, Mr. Riedlmayer. However, they said to me that this project did not exist, that this is a mosque from the 15th century or something like that, but that there is a theoretical possibility that there is part of the project documentation for the Ferhadija mosque because it was reconstructed after the 1969 earthquake, and that encouraged me to work in that direction. I submitted a request to the municipal organs of Banja Luka to let me see the project documentation for that building. I also wanted to deal with the Petricevac church and monastery in Banja Luka that had also been destroyed, and both are within the municipality where I live, so it was quite simple for me to be running around and trying to find all this. When I returned to the municipality in Banja Luka, some people laughed at me and said: What are you looking for? And then I asked Novica Vujicic to come with me. He's an architect and his rank is that of lieutenant-colonel. He also helped me in this effort. And since he is very well versed and he is the number one architect in Banja Luka, he said: There has to be this documentation because Ferhadija was reconstructed in the 1970s, and it was an architect from Sarajevo who was in charge of that project. And we spent about ten days searching for it. It was not in the archives of Banja Luka. It was God knows where. And then the project for Petricevac, we did not have such a hard time finding that. Once we got our hands on all of that, we could embark on this task more thoroughly. And I was really pleased. I never entered the mosque before. And I saw how thick the walls were, and also the minaret, how it was reconstructed, what the dimensions were, what materials were used to build it. Also the Petricevac monastery. For example, now that we're speaking of all these details, when we speak of construction materials that were used for building these buildings, for years I saw the Petricevac monastery from the highway, and I thought that it was monolithic. Later on when I saw these documents, I realised it was rather fragile. It was built of some kind of elements that are inserted into concrete for hydro isolation and the construction is pretty light, and you see that it could be demolished very easily, even mechanically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic I'm looking at the clock. I think we should take a break. Could the witness follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your last question, which was did you look for project documentation, ended up in a totally unstructured monologue of two pages, where the Chamber easily will be lost in understanding what exactly you were seeking to have established. Could I invite you to be focused in your questioning and also not to repeat many things that are found in the report already. We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was informed that I have one hour left, but I will finish before that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Formally you have one hour left. That means that you used --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hour and a half. But some of the time, which was taken by the Judges was, as a matter of fact, to correct a few shortcomings. So therefore, you are encouraged to see whether you could finish well within that hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have on our screens 1D5761, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you tendering 1D5892?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Thank you. But it's report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's coming at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- report and we do that at the end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says that this document is the ground plan of the Ferhadija mosque. You can see it on your screen; isn't that right? And I wanted to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was 1D5764, this document, before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, let's just wait till we see it in English. It says: "Plan for the restoration of the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka." At the bottom, it states 1988 as the date when the document was created. These two documents that we saw, the restoration of the mosque and the plan of the mosque, did you receive that at the same address, these two documents? They didn't hear you. Your answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. All of this was at the city administration of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document that we see in front of you -- in front of us, can we now look at page 4, please. You told us before that the Ferhadija mosque is larger than the usual mosques in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what would be the method used to demolish the Ferhadija mosque other than explosives, or did you have to use explosives? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you take into account that the Ferhadija mosque was built of stone, or limestone actually, a rock that is formed by sedimentation in cold water, in this case in Vrbas, near Banja Luka, so this is a building that, other than the limestone and mortar, has nothing else, and the building was shaken by an earthquake in 1969, and you could see the cracks in the building, and this is something that was restored later. So this building, no matter how imposing and stable it seems, I guarantee that it could have been demolished mechanically and it was not necessary to use explosives at all. There is no reinforcing bars in the building at all -- actually, there are some reinforcing bars that were used to repair the cracks that appeared on the Ferhadija after the earthquake. So there was steel bars that were used to reinforce the building, so that when the Ferhadija was mined, the minaret remained standing. These bars prevented it from completely toppling over. For a week, for seven days, it remained at an angle of some 65 degrees and it did not topple over, and that was due to the reinforcement that was used in order to repair the building after the earthquake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now like to back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to tendered these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5761 receives number D1177. And document 1D5764 receives number D1178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1177 and D1178 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go back to the document 1D5892, which is the report of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we can see your report. We're going to look at page 11 in the B/C/S and page 12 of the English version. This is the part that you entitled: "Final Preparations of the Structure for Demolition." And we can see here what these final preparations are. You talked about providing direct physical security, making the places for mine drills, drilling mine holes, drilling in walls and other load-bearing elements of the building, making and placing explosive charges, preparing the detonation stations. You did the calculations for the Ferhadija, so could please tell us whether in that particular case the demolition was conducted in this way, the preparation was done in this way, and were you able to recognise if any of this was done based on looking at the photographs which you saw in Mr. Riedlmayer's report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, isn't the answer perfectly clear in the report that this is not how it was prepared and that is not how it happened, so therefore why ask the witness again? Unless you would disagree with me, Witness, that I clearly read in your report that this is not the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it only for Ferhadija, or you consider that this answer was given for all shrines [Overlapping speakers] ... described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm focusing at this moment -- okay. Let's ask the witness. Was this, on the basis of all these calculations, did I read well in your report that this is not how the Ferhadija was prepared for destruction and finally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then move on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the other buildings that were looked at, did you come to the same conclusion as for the Ferhadija, that they were not -- the drilling was not done in the proper way? And can you please tell us what your conclusions were, how were these buildings demolished? Just wait for one second because I think my learned friend Mr. Traldi has an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like a little bit more specificity as to all the other buildings. Now, my immediate inference is that it refers to those that are included in Attachment P of the report, which is a selection of some of Mr. Riedlmayer's formatted entries as best I can tell, but I'd like it to be clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is also not used yet to the post-recess practices; that is, to switch off your phone when being in court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojkovic, did you draw your conclusions only for those buildings in your P annex or for all the buildings that were looked at by Mr. Riedlmayer, and what is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My conclusion is based on all of the 94 buildings looked at by Mr. Riedlmayer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the whole answer by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat. You started by saying your conclusion is based on all the 94 buildings looked at by Mr. Riedlmayer, and could you repeat what you then said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're not able to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, is the -- your microphone is on. Could you please again repeat what you said. Then perhaps move the microphone -- yes. Speak clearly into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I based my conclusions on all 94 demolished places of worship in the B and H territory that were looked at by Mr. Riedlmayer in his report. I studied all the documents very carefully, of course, as much as I could, by looking at the photographs and by reading what Mr. Riedlmayer wrote, and it was not all that simple to do. There is a lot missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not deal with all 94 objects in your P annex?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 94 buildings looked at by the expert, I took the most characteristic ones as far as I was concerned going by the way in which they were demolished. I looked at the demolition that was done in what I would describe as a criminal way without any particular model, system, or method.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what would be the prevalent way that this was done? What was your conclusion as to how these buildings, primarily mosques, were demolished?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases when mosques in BH were demolished, it was minarets that were attacked first and foremost, and too much explosive was being used, enough to destroy the entire building. Now, it depended on where the explosive was placed. The minaret would fall either on the building itself or to the side. Secondly, in most cases when minarets were destroyed, the roofs were damaged too. Also, in many cases after the building was destroyed, it was also torched -- or rather, it is very difficult to ascertain whether buildings were burned before or after the demolition. At any rate, explosives were placed inside the minaret and at the level of the roof, if I can put it that way. So the explosive would usually damage the roof or blow it away. And then, of course, due to the weather conditions - rain, snow, et cetera - you don't know what was destroyed by explosions and what was due simply to the passage of time and the weather conditions involved. On of the basis of photographs only, it is hard to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform Your Honours that my transcript is not working anymore for a while, and it's hard for me to follow what's being entered and what's not. But I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, and I take it that it will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to finish this way. Hopefully tomorrow we'll be in a better shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about LiveNote? Perhaps you can follow on LiveNote, the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I need that one for e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But thank you anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ask anybody else for documentation; courts, the police? Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you get from the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked for -- actually, for this facility, Ferhadija and the Petricevac church, through the Ministry of the Interior, RS. I asked for the criminal file for these two destroyed buildings, and I used up quite a bit of time because they kept sending me from the court to the SUP to the police and so on, and this went on for days too. So I studied this case file and there's nothing else but witness statements as far as the destruction of the building is concerned. However, the record also says that the on-site investigation included photo documentation; however I didn't find a single photograph. When I asked the MUP what this was all about, they told me that the prosecutor's office took over the entire case file and that that was the only thing left, and therefore I inserted that here on purpose. And nothing can be seen from these statements, literally. You just see a guard close to a cafe who said it was blown up at such and such a point in time and that is why these fragments of the mosque reached this place, and I was almost hit, and this really has nothing do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is now commenting on reports. Are they in evidence, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so, but I have to locate it exactly where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because for us to understand the evidence of the witness, we would know what he is commenting on. Because I saw also in his report that he's quite often commenting on a certain book written by -- forgive me that I've forgotten the name, which as far as I am concerned, is not in evidence. What's the use of hearing, reading comments on what is not before us? And this is, of course, now -- I also saw that the witness was complaining but not having access to certain sources. The report dates from February, and I would have expected the Defence to seek our assistance in order to get access to those sources you consider to be relevant enough to present an expert report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In -- it's Attachment N, criminal report composed by police. In B/C/S, it's page 65. I suppose it's page, in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that on your list of exhibits? Is it -- I see two criminal cases at numbers, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- third from the bottom and fourth from the bottom. Is that what these questions and these answers refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first one, the police one, is 1D5770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And the other one is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other one is court file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the logical way of approaching this is to introduce that report, then to ask the witness exactly what kind of comments he has on it, and then to tender those reports in evidence if there are, of course, no objections to it. Because now the witness is stating all kind of things about -- but that's apparently then the attachments he is commenting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- well, perhaps rather not proceed. And take your time to prepare for the last small portion of time left for tomorrow. Witness, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, and we hope to be able to conclude your testimony tomorrow. It's uncertain whether we'll be able to do it. But before you leave this courtroom, I want to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher, and we expect you back at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's anything to be raised now, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume until tomorrow, Tuesday, the 11th of August, courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of August, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
